newsitem.title: USA: NHL-DETROIT LOOKS TO END TITLE DROUGHT AGAINST OVERSIZED FLYERS.
newsitem.headline: NHL-DETROIT LOOKS TO END TITLE DROUGHT AGAINST OVERSIZED FLYERS.

text.p: Detroit hockey fans have gone 42 years without a Stanley Cup and Red Wings captain Steve Yzerman has been waiting 14 of those years to hoist hockey's holy Grail.

They get their chance to end the longest current title drought in the NHL beginning Saturday, when the best-of-seven Stanley Cup finals begin, with the only thing standing in Detroit's path -- Eric Lindros and the largest ice hockey team ever assembled.

The huge, strong, young and mean Philadelphia Flyers will do whatever is necessary to extend Detroit's frustration streak. And after Lindros and his "Legion of Doom" linemates ended the latest Stanley Cup aspirations of both Mario Lemieux and Wayne Gretzky, it seems the torch has been forcibly passed to the new prototype of superstar.
"Eric Lindros wants a championship in the worst way," said Philadelphia coach Terry Murray. "I have never seen him play as hungry as he is now."

The Flyers young captain had five goals and four assists as Philadelphia beat Gretzky's New York Rangers in five games in the Eastern Conference finals. He is tied for second in the league in playoff scoring with 23 points in 15 games.
"We have won three series, but the big one is yet to come," said Lindros. "No one remembers you if you finish second."

The image of Rangers winger Esa Tikkanen throwing his full weight into Lindros only to bounce off like a bicycle hitting a freight train is one that will not be lost on Detroit when they study Philadelphia's playoff films.

The Flyers last won the Cup in 1975, when current General Manager Bobby Clarke was the one-ice leader, and are making their first finals appearance in a decade. But it's a new Philadelphia team, averaging just 24 years of age, that will crash bodies with the Red Wings and their celebrated, free-wheeling Russian unit.

Detroit's "Russian Five" has played brilliantly and with an intensity level previously unknown from them in past playoffs. The Red Wings are 12-0 in playoff games this year in which Sergei Fedorov, Igor Larionov, Vyacheslav Kozlov, Vladimir Konstantinov or Slava Fetisov have scored.

And Detroit this season has added quality players like 47-goal scorer Brendan Shanahan to the team that was shockingly swept out of the 1995 finals by the New Jersey Devils, adding to Yzerman's frustration in leading a team that always contends for the best regular season record only to fall short year after year in the playoffs.

"The mix wasn't working so we made some changes, getting bigger and better with Shanahan, (Tomas) Sandstrom and Larry Murphy," said legendary Detroit coach Scottie Bowman, whose team upset the defending champion Colorado Avalanche in the Western Conference finals, reversing the 1996 result.

"We have to get back to the emotional high we had in the series against Colorado. It went six games and we played just about the best game we have in my four years here in the last game against Colorado," Bowman said.

Lindros centres Philadelphia's feared "Legion of Doom" line with John LeClair -- one of the league's four 50-goal scorers this season -- and Mikael Renberg, who has been hampered by an ankle injury and has lately been replaced by talented 18-year-old rookie Dainius Zubrus.

But the Flyers have stepped it up from one end of the bench to the other, getting stellar play from second-line centre Rod Brind'Amour, defenceman Eric Desjardins, veteran winger Dale Hawerchuk, making his first Stanley Cup finals appearance after 1,188 regular-season games, and Paul Coffey, who has won Cups with both Edmonton and Pittsburgh.

Even the unheralded foot soldiers have been making valuable contributions, such as huge checking line forward Trent Klatt, who personally broke two Rangers with bone-crushing, but legal checks in the previous round.
"Getting this far has been a team effort," said LeClair. "It wasn't just one guy or one line."
The goaltending matches two veterans, each something of a surprise.

Philadelphia's Ron Hextall replaced young Garth Snow in Game 2 of the Eastern Conference finals. Hextall, who has had an up and down career since winning the Conn Smythe Trophy as most valuable player of the playoffs as a rookie in 1987, is 4-0 with a 2.26 goals-against average in this year's playoffs.
Bowman opted to go with battle-tested veteran Mike Vernon, who spent the entire regular season as backup to Chris Osgood.

Vernon, who backstopped Calgary to the Stanley Cup in 1989, has started all 16 of Detroit's post-season games. And with the exception of one 6-0 blowout by Colorado, he has been superb between the pipes.

Bowman has more Stanley Cup wins than any coach in NHL history and is in the finals for the 11th time. After guiding Montreal and Pittsburgh to championships, Bowman again has a chance to become the first coach to win Cups with three different teams and give Detroit its first title since 1955.
Murray, like his team, has far less playoff experience under his belt than his opponent. This will be his first Stanley Cup Final.
